entities.name: Giuseppe Albani
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giuseppe (Andrea) Albani, born into the illustrious Albani family of Rome, emerged as a preeminent Roman Catholic Cardinal whose political acumen and conservative convictions profoundly shaped the Papal States and the broader European ecclesiastical landscape in the early 19th century. Serving as Secretary of State to Leo XII and later as a leading figure in multiple conclaves, Albani was a staunch defender of papal temporal power and traditionalist doctrines, often aligning with Austrian imperial interests to counter liberal and revolutionary currents sweeping across Europe.

Albani's influence was particularly manifest in three significant papal elections. In the 1823 conclave, he played a crucial role in the election of Leo XII, ensuring the selection of a pontiff sympathetic to conservative principles. His strategic maneuvering continued in the 1829 conclave, which resulted in the short-lived pontificate of Pius VIII. Most notably, in the 1830-1831 conclave, amidst the turmoil of the July Revolution in France and nascent liberal uprisings in Italy, Albani, as a Cardinal-Deacon, exercised significant sway, ultimately facilitating the election of Gregory XVI and actively suppressing the revolts in the Papal States through Austrian military intervention.

His legacy is intricately tied to the maintenance of the Ancien Régime in the Papal States and the Catholic Church's resistance to modernizing forces. Albani's consistent advocacy for Austrian influence in Italian affairs, particularly during the Restoration period, solidified a conservative trajectory for the papacy. His actions reinforced the alliance between the Holy See and absolute monarchies, delaying reforms and contributing to the eventual internal pressures that would lead to the Risorgimento and the end of papal temporal rule.
